slides.title: Conversation events
slides.subtitle: Read the company's ordered event log, recover a lost cursor, never deliver twice
slides.notes: After sending a message, the personal agent reads what the company did next from an ordered event log. This example follows a conversation page by page, recovers from an expired cursor, and drops events the company repeats.

slides.title: Why a cursor
slides.statement: The cursor is **opaque**: save it exactly, send it back as is, advance it only after handling the page.
slides.notes: The cursor marks how far the host has read. The host never interprets it. It moves the cursor forward only once a page has been handled, so a crash in between replays events rather than losing them.

slides.title: Who takes part
slides.diagram:
flowchart LR M["Model or product UI"] subgraph HOST["Your host, trusted"] direction TB H["PAP host
long polls"] -- "keeps" --> K[("Saved cursor
delivered event IDs")] end subgraph CO["Company"] direction TB A["Company agent
serves pages"] -- "reads" --> L[("Ordered event log")] end HOST -- "GET events, token, DPoP" --> CO HOST -. "event fields only" .-> M
slides.caption: The host does the reading and keeps the cursor; the model or UI receives only the event fields it needs.
slides.notes: Start inside the host. The PAP host long polls the company, and keeps two things to itself: the saved cursor and the IDs of the events it has already delivered. Each request crosses with the Session Token and a DPoP proof. On the company's side, its agent serves pages from an ordered event log, each with a cursor and a has_more flag. Off to the side, the model or the product's interface follows the conversation and receives only the event fields it needs, never the token, the proofs, the pairwise identity or the cursor.

slides.title: One read, start to finish
slides.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  participant H as PAP host
  participant C as Company
  H->>C: GET events, saved cursor, wait=30
  C-->>H: 410 cursor_expired
  H->>C: GET events from the beginning
  C-->>H: evt_1, evt_2, has_more
  H->>C: GET events after evt_2, wait=0
  C-->>H: evt_2 again, evt_3
  Note over H: Drop the repeated evt_2
slides.notes: The saved cursor has expired, so the host tells the person and reads once from the beginning. The page has more behind it, so the host drains the next page at once. The company repeats evt_2 after the reconnect; the host drops it and delivers only evt_3.

slides.title: What the iterator does
slides.caption: Every event delivered once, in the company's order.
slides.notes: Follow one page around the loop. An expired cursor makes the iterator call the host's cursor-expiry callback, so the person can be told, and then read once from the beginning. Otherwise it delivers the events it has not seen, in the company's order, and drops repeated IDs; the set it remembers is bounded and fails closed at the limit. While has_more is true it reads the next page at once. With no backlog, a closed conversation stops the loop, and an open one is long polled again, normally for 30 seconds. Python's events() and TypeScript's events() follow these rules; read_events and readEvents read a single page.

slides.title: When the cursor expires
slides.statement: Reading from the beginning recovers **retained** events, not the ones the company **deleted**.
slides.notes: Before its one recovery read, the iterator calls the host's cursor-expiry callback. That is where the host tells the person that part of the conversation may be missing, because nothing can bring back events the company no longer keeps.

slides.title: What stays where

right.heading: What the model or UI sees

slides.notes: Tokens, proofs, pairwise identity and the cursor stay in the trusted host. The model or the interface receives only the event fields it needs.

slides.title: Run it yourself
slides.cta: The Pydantic AI and Agent Runtimes examples follow a local conversation until it closes
slides.notes: A company that streams can be read over SSE instead, with reconnects and display-only text deltas. That is the conversation streaming example.
